description.narrative: Capacity of State Labour Department in Telengana enhanced for implementation of integrated framework of Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work in collaboration with other government departments in the states. Farmer-Producer Organizations (FPOs) incorporated FPRW as their mandate by amending the by-laws ; Collectivization of farmers and workers promoted through awareness on collective bargaining – leading to initiatives beyond the cotton sector (about 11,000 members formed Telangana Cotton Workers and Small Farmers and Migrant Workers Trade Union Congress; Government of Telangana developed and disseminated communication material for raising awareness on FPRW and elimination of child labour in the state. The ILO supported creation of platform for collaboration between local administration, trade union, implementation partner and cotton farmers/workers in the state of Telangana. Training of more than 32,000 participants across state, districts and villages on the pillars of FPRW. Rounds of dialogues and negotiations facilitated between buyers and sellers in the supply chain on prices and other critical inputs support, enhancing absorption capacity of the farmers to address FPRW issues. Collectivization of farmers and workers promoted through awareness on collective bargaining.

description.narrative:
Capacity of stakeholders in Jharkhand State enhanced for elimination of child labour with a focus on Occupational Safety and Health in minor minerals, improved understanding of Labour Laws, forest conservation and sustainable environment. The Government of Jharkhand has formally launched the new 'Dhibra policy' in the mica district of Koderma in March 2022. The Dhibra policy is a cooperatives policy formulated for the welfare of Mica mining workers. It aims to formalize mica mining through a cooperatives model where the aggregated mica mineral is collected at the local panchayat. The bidding process is administered by the Jharkhand State Mineral Development Corporation (JSMDC).
The government of India demonstrated its increased commitment to elimination of child labour through its participation in the Global Conference on Child Labour in 2022. The Joint Secretary made a public statement to ending child labour in India. ILO social partners participated in the India SDG 8.7 platform which endeavours to accelerate progress towards eliminating child and forced labour in India. They developed their capacity and commitment through regular meetings and technical sessions while also sharing their experiences .
"Benefit Package" report on government services of Government of India relevant for child labour families designed and outreach services targeting child labour families undertaken. Eight government schemes selected targeting 200 child labour families in Bihar through a unique model of convergence in collaboration with local administration, trade union, skill training centre and civil society organisation. Community volunteers trained and engaged to empower families through outreach services linking eligible child labour families with government services. The ILO t funded by the FCDO provided technical assistance to stakeholders involved in the policy formulation at various stages. ILO brought stakeholders together for a discourse on decent work deficit in dhibra picking (and the supply chain for Mica). A white paper is being developed by ILO on Decent Work in Mica Supply Chain in line with the five pillars of FPRW. The combined efforts of mapping of evidence, community empowerment, and systemic change efforts on living income are foreseen to contribute towards accomplishing SDG Target 8.7 grounded in the principles of FPRW. This white paper will be an advocacy tool for the stakeholders to formalize the mica mining at the local level. ILO's tools for child labour which was incorporated in the village development plans. The ILO convened the Global Conference on Child Labour and ensured that the Government, at senior level participated in it. Two joint secretaries participated in the conference. The ILO also convener for the India SDG 8.7 Platform Workers Information and Support Centre (WISC) a trade union hub supported by ILO for information and support services including trainings for vulnerable and crisis affected workers facilitated skill training by linkages with Government of India Skill Mission for non-literates, neo-literates as well as school dropouts in target areas With the Support of the US Department of Labour in India.

description.narrative:
The Government of India, together with employers’ and workers’ organizations, developed, implemented, and advocated for best practices in the ship recycling sector, in following-up to the recommendations adopted at the National Tripartite Workshop on Improving Occupational Safety and Health, organized by the ILO in Mumbai, Maharashtra, on 26-27 September 2019 and in accordance with the ILO’s Safety and health in ship breaking: Guidelines for Asian Countries and Turkey, 2004.
Action in this area focuses on enhancing the skills and awareness of ship recyclers and workers within ship recycling yards and downstream operations to improve OSH performance. In particular:
- An industry-wide tripartite safety and health committee in ship recycling sector was established with participation of the Directorate General of Shipping, the industry, Gujarat Maritime Board (GMB) and Alang Sosiya Ship Recycling & General Workers' Association (ASSRGWA). - ASSRGWA's support led to the unionization of 345 recycling downstream workers for the first time. This has enabled them to access social protection benefits through registration in e-Shram and other social protection schemes. - 105 individuals, representing safety and health committees from all 45 operational yards (supported by Ship Recycling Industries Association -SRIA), participated in the ILO Training of Trainers on safety and health.
A tripartite workshop adopted a draft report listing major recommendations for improving the situation of sanitation workers in India. The recommendations include expanding the scope of the current legislative tools and developing guidelines to promote safe working conditions for women workers. The ILO places strong emphasis on the sustainability of the initiatives on ship recycling in India, which involve multiple stakeholders to enhance working conditions and foster high-quality employment prospects across the ship recycling supply chains.
With support from DG Shipping, GMB, SRIA, and ASSRGWA, the ILO has developed an action plan for a just transition and is implementing it to promote OSH and decent jobs in the ship recycling industry.
Additionally, a pocket diary capturing existing welfare schemes of the Government for ship recycling downstream workers in Alang has been published and distributed.
A draft report on situational assessment of sanitation workers with a focus on manual scavengers has been prepared by the ILO. The report uncovers the situation of sanitation workers in India and examines the current legislative framework that seeks to protect these workers. This examination is supplemented by interviews with representative employers’ organizations, workers’ organizations and government departments working directly with such workers.

description.narrative: To strengthen domestic systems on preventing and eliminating violence and harassment against women in the world of work, the Supreme Court of India issued guidelines for proper implementation of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 on 23 May 2023. To enhance the capacity of trade unions to promote a world of work free from violence and harassment, trade unions underwent a Training of Trainers programme. The trained trainers of the Workers' Information and Support Centres in Bihar, Tamil Nadu, Delhi and Maharashtra, sensitised over 17,466 workers, 7,718 of whom were women, on violence and harassment at world of work, including reporting cases of violation of labour rights. One trade union, Indian National Trade Union Congress (INTUC) has initiated the process of developing a gender equality policy and a policy on harassment for adoption at the national level. Moreover, to strengthen reporting and ensuring the effective application in practice of Convention No. 190, trade union leaders also embarked on mobilisation and awareness campaigns with a view to supporting and encouraging more workers to report cases of violence and harassment to local complaints committee (LCC) in the Raigad district of Maharashtra. These efforts resulted in the trade union Hind Mazdoor Sabha (HMS) supporting the reporting of 3 cases, which were reviewed by the labour court in favour of the expelled workers. To support the ratification of Convention No. 190, individual advocates from employers’ and workers’ organisations created and disseminated audio-video messages highlighting the need to ratify the Convention and to promote a world of work free from violence and harassment for all workers. ILO provided technical support to all India Organizations of Employers and Employers Federation of India, through organising consultations on Convention No. 190. The ILO facilitated training sessions on gender discrimination, violence, and harassment for 150 trainers identified by trade unions in four states of India (Bihar, Tamil Nadu, Delhi, and Maharashtra). ILO provided technical support to unions in the development of a plan to reach out to more than 17,000 unorganized workers (construction workers, plantation workers, care workers, including domestic workers, industrial workers, self-employed weavers, street vendors) in India to sensitise them on key labour rights, register them in and raise their awareness on current social security schemes and provide them with leadership training skills. The ILO with funding from Japan also worked to advocate for the proper implementation of the Sexual Harassment Act 2013. This contribution led to the development and the issuing of the guidelines by the Supreme Court of India.
